title: Data frames, data input/output, graphics and plots in R
breadcrumb: Module 9 · R Programming · Data frames, I/O and graphics
objectives: Create and inspect data frames and select rows and columns.
Understand recycling and equal-length column requirements.
Read common data import and export functions.
Interpret plot(), hist(), boxplot(), barplot() and graphical arguments.
Distinguish plot types, axes, labels and graphical device output.

prereq.name: Vectors and lists
prereq.why: Data frames are list-like objects with equal-length columns.

prereq.name: Indexing and logical conditions
prereq.why: Rows and columns are selected with indices and conditions.

prereq.name: Basic descriptive statistics
prereq.why: Plots and summaries describe observed data.

traps: A data frame is a list of variables with equal-length columns.
data.frame() may recycle shorter columns only when lengths are compatible, such as a divisor; otherwise it errors.
df[row,column] uses row first and column second.
df$var selects a column; df[ , 'var', drop=FALSE] can preserve a data-frame result.
read.csv() imports comma-separated data; write.csv() exports it.
read.table() is a general delimited text reader.
plot() is generic; output depends on object classes and method.
hist() displays a frequency distribution; boxplot() summarises median, quartiles and potential outliers.
barplot() displays bar heights; plot(type='l') draws lines.
Graphical labels use main, xlab and ylab; axes and limits can be controlled.

sheet: data.frame(x,y) combines equal-length columns into a rectangular object.
nrow(df), ncol(df), dim(df), names(df) inspect structure.
df[i,j] selects rows then columns; df$var selects a column.
df[df$score>50,] selects rows using a logical condition.
Use drop=FALSE to preserve a one-column data-frame result.
read.table(file,header=TRUE) imports general delimited text data.
write.csv(df,file,row.names=FALSE) exports a CSV without row names.
plot(x,y) creates a scatter plot by default for numeric vectors.
hist(x) shows a frequency distribution; boxplot(x) shows a five-number summary and potential outliers.
barplot(height) displays bar heights; plot(x,type='l') draws a line plot.
main, xlab and ylab set title and axis labels.
tricks: Check equal column lengths before data.frame().
Remember row index first, column index second.
Use row.names=FALSE for clean CSV export.
Match plot type to variable structure.
shortcuts: Write row and column subscripts explicitly.
Choose histogram for one numeric variable.
Choose scatter plot for two numeric variables.
remember: hist is distribution; boxplot is spread; scatter plot is relationship.
main, xlab and ylab label a plot.

howto: Inspect a data frame with dim(), names() and str(). Select rows and columns deliberately. Choose an import/export function based on the file format. For plots, identify variable types and the question before selecting a graph, then label axes and title.

scenes.title: A data frame is a rectangular object
body: A data frame stores variables as columns. Each column has the same number of rows, while different columns may have different types.
Use data.frame() to combine vectors into columns. Inspect dimensions with dim(), nrow() and ncol().
Use names() and str() to inspect variable names and structure.

items.recall: A rectangular object whose columns have compatible equal lengths.
refresh: A data frame is a list-like rectangular structure in which each variable is stored as a column. Each column has one entry per row, although different columns can have different data types.
Use dim(), nrow(), ncol(), names() and str() to inspect the object before selecting observations. This confirms the dimensions, variables and storage types used in subsequent expressions.

items.ask: In df[i,j], what is indexed first?
items.recall: Rows are indexed first, then columns.
refresh: The first subscript in df[i,j] selects rows and the second selects columns. A blank row or column position means that all entries in that dimension are retained.
For a logical filter, construct the condition from a column and place it in the row position, such as df[df$score>50,]. This returns the observations satisfying the condition.

items.ask: Which function imports a comma-separated file?
refresh: read.csv() reads a comma-separated values file and returns a data frame by default. It is a convenient choice when the first line contains variable names.
The corresponding export function is write.csv(). When exporting a data frame for reuse, consider row.names=FALSE so that row numbers are not written as an additional data column.

ask.q: Which function displays a data frame's structure?

scenes.title: Rows and columns answer different questions
body: df[i,j] selects rows first and columns second. df$score extracts the score column.
A logical row condition such as df[df$score>50,] selects observations satisfying the condition.

scenario.title: A tutor selects qualifying students
body: A tutor has a data frame with name and score columns. To select students scoring above 50, the row condition is applied to the score column.
The result contains complete rows for qualifying students, not just the score values.

Before sharing the result, the analyst should inspect the dimensions and variable names, check that the filter selects the intended records, and label the graph so its variables and units are clear. The chosen plot should answer the analytical question rather than simply display whatever data structure is easiest to pass to a plotting function.

ask.q: In df[i,j], what does i represent?

blocks.body: data.frame(id=c(1,2),score=c(70,85)) creates two columns and two rows.
df[i,j] selects rows i and columns j. df$score selects the named column.
Use drop=FALSE when a subset should remain a data frame, especially when one column is selected.

ask.q: How do you select the score column by name?

scenes.problem: df=data.frame(id=1:3,score=c(40,60,80)). How many rows and columns? Which ids have score>50?

steps.why: Each vector has length 3 and there are two variables.

items.a: Export a data frame to CSV.

ask.q: Which function imports a CSV file?

blocks.body: read.csv('data.csv') reads comma-separated values and treats the first row as column names by default.
read.table() reads tabular text and provides arguments such as header and sep.
write.csv(df,'out.csv',row.names=FALSE) writes data without an extra row-name column.

ask.q: How do you prevent row names from being written to CSV?

hints: Set row.names=FALSE in the export call.

solution.why: The id and score vectors each contain three entries.
Only the second and third scores exceed 50.

blocks.body: hist(x) displays the frequency distribution of one quantitative variable.
boxplot(x) displays median, quartiles, spread and potential outliers.
plot(x,y) displays paired numeric values; plot(x,type='l') draws a line plot.

ask.q: Which plot is suitable for the relationship between two numeric variables?
ask.nudge: Plot paired x and y values.

scenes.problem: You have numeric vectors age and income and want to examine their relationship with a title and axis labels. Give a suitable call.
hints: Use plot(age,income) for paired numeric values.
Set xlab and ylab for axis labels.

scenario.title: An analyst studies age and income
body: An analyst wants to examine whether income changes with age. Both variables are numeric, so paired observations should be displayed in a scatter plot.
A meaningful title and axis labels make the graph interpretable.

Before sharing the result, the analyst should inspect the dimensions and variable names, check that the filter selects the intended records, and label the graph so its variables and units are clear. The chosen plot should answer the analytical question rather than simply display whatever data structure is easiest to pass to a plotting function.

ask.q: Which argument sets the y-axis label?

solution.math: age and income are both numeric vectors.
solution.why: The question asks about paired observations on two quantitative variables.
The default plot for two numeric vectors is a scatter plot.
A title and axis labels make the variables and relationship clear.

items.why: A histogram displays the distribution of one quantitative variable.

scenes.title: Data frames, I/O and graphics quick sheet
body: A data frame is a rectangular list of equal-length columns. Inspect with dim(), names() and str().
df[i,j] selects rows then columns; df$var selects a column. Use drop=FALSE to preserve a data-frame subset.
read.csv() and read.table() import data; write.csv() exports it. Set row.names=FALSE when needed.
hist() shows a univariate distribution; boxplot() summarises spread and potential outliers.
plot(x,y) displays paired numeric values; plot(x,type='l') draws lines; barplot() displays bar heights.
Use main, xlab and ylab for title and axis labels.

ask.q: Match histogram and scatter plot to their data structures.
ask.nudge: One numeric variable versus paired numeric variables.
